consensus_summary: The blind consensus holds that the symbolic 'beast' represents earthly political power in opposition to God — kingdoms, empires, or their rulers (Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome; the beast of Revelation as Antichrist/Rome/Nero), i.e., brutal, idolatrous, satanically empowered human government that persecutes God's people. Alternatives include an individual Antichrist, Nero/Rome, the papacy, timeless evil power, degraded human nature, chaos forces, and (minority, in Response C) unclean animals signifying Gentiles/outsiders per Acts 10.
book_summary: The book defines beast as a nation or kingdom organized under earthly rule, often shown in its wild or predatory character; different beasts distinguish different kingdoms, and clean vs. unclean beasts distinguish kinds of people (citing Dan 7:17; 8:20-21; Acts 10:12, 28).
consensus_core_identification: Beast = a God-opposing, oppressive earthly kingdom/empire or its ruler, empowered by Satan and persecuting God's people (chiefly in Daniel and Revelation apocalyptic).
book_core_identification: Beast = a nation or kingdom under earthly rule as such (with wildness/predation a frequent but not defining trait), plus a second sense: clean/unclean beasts = kinds of people (Jew/Gentile distinction).
boundary_disagreement: The consensus makes anti-God hostility, persecution, and satanic empowerment constitutive of the beast symbol; the book makes the referent simply any nation/kingdom organized under earthly rule, with predatory character as a frequent characteristic rather than a defining condition. The book thus admits kingdoms generally, not only God-opposing ones. Additionally, the book elevates the clean/unclean-beasts-as-kinds-of-people reading (Acts 10) — only a minority alternative in Response C and absent from A, B, and D — into part of the primary definition.
rationale: Both readings center on the same referent: beasts symbolize kingdoms/kings, an identification given within Scripture itself (Dan 7:17). The book preserves this core but broadens it by dropping the consensus's defining specification (opposition to God, persecution, satanic empowerment, Antichrist association) and softening predation to an incidental trait ('often shown'). It further extends the term's coverage by incorporating the clean/unclean distinction as a classification of kinds of people, a case most consensus responses treat as marginal or omit entirely. This is a real boundary change — the book's beast covers earthly polities as such and human classifications — but the central category (earthly kingdoms) is retained, so the relation is REFINED, not DIVERGENT.
strongest_objection: One could argue MATCH: Dan 7:17 and 7:23 are the shared proof texts, the consensus itself acknowledges the general 'kingdom/king' meaning as the settled core, and the book's 'wild or predatory character' implicitly carries the hostility element, making the differences mere wording. The Acts 10 sense is also present as a listed alternative in Response C, so nothing in the book is outside consensus coverage.
